about.heading: About
paragraphs: I'm a senior software engineer with a decade of experience turning complex ideas into production-ready systems. My core stack is C#/.NET and Node.js for secure, cloud-native backends and React for responsive, user-friendly UIs.

I've built and optimized platforms in e-commerce, logistics, and energy trading. I enjoy shaping ambiguous requirements into real solutions and taking full ownership of the software lifecycle: from design and development to deployment, monitoring, and support.

Beyond coding, I contribute by leading architecture discussions, running code reviews, and mentoring engineers, helping teams align and grow. What excites me most is building software that not only scales but also empowers businesses to move faster with confidence.

plainlysmart.description: Bilingual marketing website for a custom software business, built as a fully static Next.js application with localized content, interactive consultation flows, bot protection and campaign attribution

details.overview: PlainlySmart started as a simple marketing website for a custom software business, but I deliberately treated it as a production application rather than a collection of static pages. The goal was to keep the frontend completely statically deployable while still supporting localization, theme persistence, interactive consultation flows, campaign attribution and secure communication with an external backend. The result is a lightweight Next.js site that does not require a Node.js server at runtime, while still behaving like a modern application in the browser.
role: I designed and built the site end to end, from the visual structure and responsive components to localization, browser-side state, accessibility and the contact workflow. I used Next.js App Router with TypeScript and Tailwind CSS 4, then added Motion selectively to make the interface feel more dynamic without turning animation into a dependency for usability.

As the project evolved, I moved the contact flow away from simple email links into a reusable consultation dialog. React Hook Form now owns form state, Zod owns validation and normalization, and next-intl provides localized validation messages, keeping each responsibility explicit instead of accumulating form logic in one component.

I also designed the integration boundary for a separate contact API. The static frontend collects the lead, attaches locale and campaign attribution, obtains a Cloudflare Turnstile token and sends the request to an external endpoint, allowing the frontend and backend infrastructure to evolve independently.
architecture: The application is exported as static HTML, CSS and JavaScript, so it can be hosted without a Next.js server. Dynamic operations such as contact submission are pushed behind external APIs instead of relying on Next.js server routes.

Localization is handled with next-intl using symmetrical /en and /cs routes. Explicit URLs take precedence over browser detection, language preferences are persisted client-side and theme state is preserved across locale switches without introducing hydration mismatches.

The consultation experience is shared across the page through React Context. Individual CTAs can open the same native dialog without prop drilling, while the dialog lifecycle remains separate from the form implementation.

The contact form uses React Hook Form together with a Zod schema. Zod trims and validates submitted values, React Hook Form handles field registration, validation errors and submission state, and accessible error relationships are provided through aria-invalid and aria-describedby.

Cloudflare Turnstile is integrated through its explicit JavaScript API. A small React wrapper loads the external script, renders the widget through window.turnstile.render, propagates verification tokens to the parent form and recreates the widget when a failed submission requires a fresh token.

Campaign attribution is captured from standard UTM parameters and persisted in sessionStorage with an in-memory fallback. The values follow the visitor through navigation and are attached to the eventual contact request together with the current locale.

Playwright browser tests cover the static export rather than only the development server, including localization, theme persistence, blocked storage scenarios, navigation behaviour and browser-level JavaScript errors.
challenges: One of the main design decisions was keeping the site truly static without giving up application-like behaviour. Instead of introducing a Next.js runtime just for one form, I separated the frontend from the future contact backend and designed the browser to communicate with a dedicated API endpoint.

Localization introduced more complexity than translating strings. The site had to choose the correct language on the first visit, preserve explicit locale URLs, remember user preferences, survive unavailable browser storage and keep dark mode stable across full locale navigation without hydration flashes.

The consultation form gradually accumulated validation, duplicate-submission protection, status handling and data extraction logic. Refactoring it around React Hook Form and Zod simplified the component by giving form state and validation clear owners while leaving Turnstile, tracking and API submission as application concerns.

Integrating Turnstile required bridging React's declarative lifecycle with an imperative third-party API. The component has to wait for the external script, render into a referenced DOM element, clean up the previous widget and deliberately recreate it when a verification token becomes unusable.

UTM tracking also needed to work defensively. Browser storage may be unavailable, stored JSON cannot be trusted and campaign values need to survive client-side navigation, so the implementation validates restored data and falls back to in-memory state instead of allowing tracking code to interfere with the actual contact flow.
results: The project evolved from a static company landing page into a production-oriented marketing application while retaining a fully static deployment model.
Visitors can move between English and Czech versions, preserve their theme preferences and open the same consultation experience from multiple areas of the site without duplicating dialog logic.

The contact workflow now has typed form state, schema-driven validation, localized errors, Turnstile verification, UTM attribution and a clean boundary for an external API rather than relying on mailto-based submission.
The architecture leaves room for the backend to be introduced independently, for example through AWS API Gateway and Lambda, without changing the static hosting model of the frontend.

The project also gave me a practical environment for working through issues that tend to be hidden in simpler marketing sites: hydration behaviour, accessibility, browser storage failures, third-party script lifecycles, static-export testing and client-to-server trust boundaries.

hostomat.description: NestJS API for accommodation providers to manage bookings and collect guest registration details through secure, shareable links

details.overview: Hostomat is a backend application for accommodation providers that manages accommodations and bookings while simplifying guest registration through secure, shareable registration links. It separates host-facing administration from guest-facing registration flows and is designed as a foundation for automating accommodation reporting workflows.
role: Designed and developed the application architecture and REST API with NestJS and TypeScript.
Implemented domain workflows for hosts, accommodations, bookings, coordinator sessions, guest sessions, and guest registrations.
Built MongoDB persistence with Mongoose and automated testing with Jest, including end-to-end coverage of complete registration flows.
architecture: Modular NestJS REST API with TypeScript
MongoDB persistence through Mongoose repositories and domain-oriented models
Authenticated host workflows for managing accommodations and bookings
Token-based coordinator and guest sessions for secure, limited-access registration flows
Separation between host administration and public guest-registration endpoints
Unit and end-to-end testing with Jest against an isolated test database
challenges: Designing a registration flow that allows guests to submit personal details without requiring an account while keeping access scoped and secure.
Modelling the lifecycle between bookings, coordinator sessions, guest sessions, and completed registrations without tightly coupling the individual workflows.
Keeping persistence concerns isolated from application logic while working with MongoDB and Mongoose.
Testing multi-step workflows end to end, including authentication, session creation, registration completion, and database state changes.
results: Built a working API foundation covering the complete flow from host onboarding and booking creation to guest registration.
Created a secure shareable-link workflow that lets accommodation providers collect registration details directly from guests.
Established automated test coverage for critical application and persistence workflows.
Created an extensible backend foundation for future accommodation reporting and city-tax automation.

personal-portfolio.description: Bilingual portfolio built with Next.js, combining detailed project stories with static hosting, language-aware navigation and persistent theme preferences

details.overview: I built this portfolio to give my work more context than a CV can provide. Alongside experience and skills, it brings individual projects into focus through stories about the problems, implementation choices and outcomes behind them. Building it also became an opportunity to work through the details of a bilingual Next.js application that can be deployed entirely as static files.
role: I developed the site with Next.js App Router, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, creating reusable components for project cards, technology lists, navigation and case-study pages. I kept the portfolio content in structured JSON so that adding a project or updating my experience would flow through the existing pages without requiring a new layout each time.

I extended the experience with English and Czech routes, language switching and persistent theme preferences. To check how those features behave after deployment, I added Playwright coverage for locale selection, navigation, browser storage restrictions and the generated static pages.
architecture: The site generates its pages at build time and exports HTML, CSS and JavaScript for static hosting. Typed content files supply each language's portfolio data, while next-intl handles shared interface text and locale-aware navigation. Project detail routes are generated from the slugs in the content, connecting the project listing and individual stories through the same data model.

English and Czech pages live under explicit /en and /cs URLs. A separate entry page chooses a language in the browser using a saved preference, supported browser languages and an English fallback. Separate root layouts give the exported pages the correct document language, while a shared document component integrates theme initialization. Localized metadata provides canonical URLs and language alternatives.
challenges: The main challenge was making language selection feel natural within a static deployment. A visitor opening a direct link needs to see the language in that URL, even if their browser or saved preference suggests another one. I kept automatic detection at the root entry point and made explicit language switches remember the visitor's choice while preserving the current path, query parameters and fragment.

Preferences also needed to survive the less convenient cases: browser storage can be blocked, and switching between locale layouts can affect theme initialization. I added defensive storage handling and shared theme setup, then covered those interactions in browser tests. Testing the actual export helped check the behaviour visitors receive from static hosting, including document language, metadata and favicon links.
results: The result is a portfolio that connects a concise introduction with deeper project stories, experience and learning history. Its reusable page structure lets the content grow through data changes, while the static export keeps deployment independent of a running Node.js server.

The project also gave me a practical way to bring localization, browser preferences and static rendering together. Automated checks now cover the supporting behaviour that is easy to overlook when reviewing a page visually, from language resolution to navigation and exported document attributes.

tubester.description: Full-stack SaaS for YouTube creators that uses AI to improve video metadata and automate comment management

details.overview: Tubester is a full-stack SaaS for YouTube creators that combines AI-assisted video optimisation with automated comment management. It integrates directly with YouTube to synchronise channel data, improve video metadata, generate contextual comment replies, and manage creator workflows from a single application.
role: Designed and built the product end to end, including the .NET backend, React and TypeScript frontend, PostgreSQL data model, background workers, external integrations, and deployment infrastructure.
Implemented Google OAuth and YouTube API integration, AI-powered workflows, retrieval-augmented generation, asynchronous background processing, CI/CD, and production observability.
architecture: ASP.NET Core backend with a React and TypeScript client
PostgreSQL persistence with EF Core and pgvector for vector similarity search
Two-stage Google OAuth flow using progressive consent: read-only YouTube access during initial onboarding, with write permissions requested only when write-enabled features are used
Hangfire background jobs for channel synchronisation, comment scanning, AI processing, and other long-running workloads
AI-assisted video metadata generation and contextual comment replies using RAG over creator-specific content
Docker-based services deployed to Kubernetes with automated CI/CD through GitHub Actions
Structured logging and production observability using Serilog, Prometheus, Loki, and Grafana
challenges: Integrating OAuth-protected YouTube operations while correctly handling user permissions, API scopes, token-dependent workflows, and external API constraints.
Designing long-running AI and YouTube operations as resilient background jobs instead of blocking interactive HTTP requests.
Building a RAG pipeline that retrieves relevant creator-specific context from PostgreSQL and pgvector to produce more useful AI-generated replies.
Operating a multi-service application in Kubernetes with sufficient logging, metrics, and observability to diagnose failures outside the local development environment.
decisions: YouTube permissions use a two-stage OAuth flow: users initially grant read-only access, while write access is requested separately only when they use features that modify YouTube data. This reduces the initial permission footprint and follows the principle of least privilege.
Long-running and failure-prone YouTube and AI operations are processed asynchronously through background jobs, keeping HTTP endpoints responsive and allowing work to be retried independently.
PostgreSQL with pgvector is used for both relational application data and vector search, avoiding the operational complexity of introducing a separate vector database.
Structured logs, metrics, and dashboards are treated as part of the application architecture rather than added only for debugging.
results: Built and deployed a functional end-to-end SaaS that synchronises real YouTube channel data and supports AI-assisted metadata optimisation and comment reply workflows.
Created a production-style architecture covering authentication, third-party APIs, asynchronous processing, vector search, CI/CD, Kubernetes deployment, and observability.

tubester.name: Tubester

i18n-process-tools.description: Localization platform that synchronizes UI labels from GitLab and GitHub repositories, manages bulk translation workflows, and writes completed React, .NET and Kotlin resources back through automated merge or pull requests.

details.overview: I18n Process Tools automated the localization lifecycle across multiple application repositories. It discovered and parsed localization resources, synchronized labels with persisted state, identified content requiring translation, grouped work into bulk requests, and turned completed translations into reviewable source-control changes. I was an early core contributor to the backend and later contributed extensively to the React frontend, working on the project from its foundational synchronization and data-model work through its GitHub migration and expansion to 30+ languages.
role: Early core contributor to the .NET backend, implementing foundational repository synchronization, project initialization, translation-state tracking, and bulk translation workflow infrastructure.
Implemented the original GitLab integration for discovering and parsing localization resources, synchronizing repository changes, and creating merge requests containing translated files.

Built and evolved the synchronization and bulk workflow, including Dirty, Pending and Translated label states, selectable target languages, label context, validation, and translation callback processing.

Introduced GitHub support with an abstraction over Git providers, Octokit-based repository operations, OAuth authentication and persisted user access tokens during the company's migration from GitLab.
Contributed to backend search, filtering, paging, authorization, validation, integration testing, Azure authentication and deployment hardening.

One of two developers contributing to the React frontend, where I implemented selectable translation languages, custom AG Grid components, label context, reusable API error handling, form validation and support for 30+ languages.
architecture: ASP.NET Core backend with application, domain, integration and persistence layers
Entity Framework Core with SQL Server persistence for projects, files, labels, bulks, mutations and translation state
Resource-specific parsing and generation for React JSON, .NET RESX and Kotlin XML localization files
React 19 and TypeScript frontend using TanStack Query, React Hook Form, AG Grid and generated Orval API clients
Git provider abstraction supporting GitLab APIs and an Octokit-based GitHub implementation
Bulk integration with Notino's Localization Service and TargetProcess, with callback-based translation processing and optional automated translation paths
Azure AD authentication, Azure Workload Identity, Docker and Kubernetes deployment
challenges: Keeping persisted localization state synchronized with changing repository files across multiple projects, languages and resource formats.
Tracking individual labels through untranslated, pending and translated states while allowing users to request only selected target languages.
Handling localization edge cases such as duplicate keys, default-language conflicts, special characters, missing target files and differences between JSON, RESX and XML resources.
Extending repository automation from GitLab to GitHub without changing the higher-level localization workflow.
Presenting large language and label sets in the frontend while keeping selection, validation and API error handling understandable.
decisions: Model translation as an explicit state machine around Dirty, Pending and Translated labels. The additional state management made synchronization more complex, but made outstanding and in-progress translation work deterministic and prevented duplicate requests.

Separate localization-resource handling by format instead of embedding parsing and generation logic directly into the synchronization workflow. This allowed the same workflow to support React JSON, .NET RESX and Kotlin XML resources.

Deliver generated translations through dedicated branches and automated merge or pull requests rather than modifying repositories directly. This kept localization changes reviewable, auditable and consistent with normal engineering workflows.

Abstract source-control operations behind a Git provider layer when adding GitHub support. The provider-specific implementation added complexity, but allowed the localization workflow to remain largely independent of GitLab or GitHub.

Use generated TypeScript API clients together with TanStack Query and reusable UI components for the frontend translation workflow, keeping API contracts typed while isolating grid selection, validation and error-handling concerns.
results: Automated the workflow from repository synchronization through translation requests, callbacks and reviewable translated source changes.
Supported localization resources across React JSON, .NET RESX and Kotlin XML projects.
Enabled translation delivery through both GitLab merge requests and GitHub pull requests.
Expanded the frontend and translation workflow to support 30+ languages with per-language selection.
Established a consistent localization workflow that could be reused across multiple application repositories and markets.

logistics-order-service.description: Event-driven .NET logistics platform for order fulfillment and warehouse operations, built around durable background processing, reliable Kafka and Azure Service Bus messaging, explicit transaction control, and operational tooling.

details.overview: A reliability-focused logistics platform supporting order fulfillment, packing, shipping and warehouse operations. The system combines transactional SQL data changes with durable background work, Kafka and Azure Service Bus messaging, dead-letter processing, scheduled jobs and production observability. I contributed across the backend and React operations UI, from reusable messaging and persistent-task infrastructure to end-to-end logistics workflows such as customs processing and transport outage management.
role: Designed and implemented a SQL-backed persistent-task mechanism for durable background work, including worker processing, retries, failure reprocessing and deadlock-prevention improvements.

Led major messaging improvements, including Azure Service Bus CloudEvent infrastructure and the migration from custom Kafka integration to the company-standard messaging library with persistent dead-letter handling and reprocessing.
Implemented end-to-end event-driven logistics flows spanning Kafka consumers, application logic, persistence, durable tasks, outbound commands, infrastructure configuration and integration tests.
Contributed to order fulfillment, packing, package allocation, transport outages, archiving, authentication and operational infrastructure across the backend.
Implemented frontend functionality for transport outage management and per-country feature toggles using React, TypeScript, React Hook Form and AG Grid.
Contributed to frontend infrastructure including generated OpenAPI clients, authentication, user permissions, multi-environment configuration and localized operational interfaces.
architecture: ASP.NET Core APIs and worker services for logistics and warehouse workflows
SQL Server persistence with explicit transaction boundaries for reliability-critical operations
SQL-backed persistent tasks with scheduled Hangfire processing, retries, reprocessing and concurrent worker coordination
Kafka and Confluent messaging through the company-standard messaging library with persistent dead-letter handling
Azure Service Bus publishers and consumers using CloudEvents and typed message handlers
React 19 and TypeScript operations UI using TanStack Query, React Hook Form, AG Grid and Orval-generated API clients
Role-based frontend and backend authorization for operational functionality
Kubernetes deployment, workload identity, environment-specific configuration, health checks, metrics and New Relic observability
challenges: Keep database changes and asynchronous follow-up work consistent so that successful business operations could not silently lose required background processing.
Safely retry failed background and messaging work without creating duplicate side effects or permanently blocking message processing.
Coordinate concurrent workers processing durable tasks while avoiding duplicate claims, abandoned work and database deadlocks.
Migrate production Kafka workloads from custom infrastructure to a shared messaging library while addressing early concurrency, performance and operational issues.
Implement logistics workflows that crossed message consumers, domain logic, SQL persistence, background workers and external integrations.
Build operational UI workflows that remained manageable across multiple countries, transports, permissions and environment-specific configurations.
decisions: Persist slower follow-up work as durable tasks instead of completing everything synchronously inside message handlers. Related business changes and tasks could be stored within the same transaction, preventing successful data changes from losing required downstream work.

Process persistent tasks through scheduled workers with explicit task state, retries and recovery. Atomic task claiming allowed multiple workers to operate concurrently while later deadlock-prevention changes hardened the processing model.

Persist failed Kafka messages and reprocess them through dedicated dead-letter workflows rather than relying only on immediate retries. This made failures recoverable and observable without blocking normal message consumption.

Use explicit event contracts and typed handlers for Kafka and Azure Service Bus integrations. This made supported event types intentional and kept transport-specific concerns separated from application processing.

Generate frontend API clients from OpenAPI contracts and build operational screens around reusable React forms and AG Grid components. This kept frontend/backend contracts typed while supporting complex country-specific editing and validation.
results: Established durable background processing with persisted state, retries, recovery and protection against abandoned or concurrently claimed work.
Migrated Kafka processing to the company-standard messaging platform and added persistent dead-letter storage, reprocessing, health checks and operational metrics.
Implemented reusable Azure Service Bus CloudEvent infrastructure for publishing and consuming logistics events.
Delivered end-to-end event-driven logistics functionality spanning message ingestion, business logic, SQL persistence, background execution, outbound commands and integration tests.
Extended operational tooling with transport outage management, country-specific feature configuration and role-aware React interfaces.
Improved the service's operational resilience through authentication, workload identity, environment configuration, health monitoring and production observability.
